title: Why One 'Quick Message Check' Destroys 23 Minutes of IQ

description_hook: Checking a notification for 30 seconds never costs just 30 seconds. Prof. Sophie Leroy's Attention Residue research explains why task-switching leaves cognitive static for 23 minutes - and the simple physical rule to fix it.

scenes.headline: A 30-Second Glance Costs 23 Minutes
bullets: Quick message checks feel harmless in the moment
Lab data shows each switch fractures deep focus for 23 minutes
scenes.narration: Glancing at a single notification for thirty seconds does not cost you thirty seconds. Research shows it hijacks the next twenty-three minutes of your cognitive sharpness.

scenes.headline: Prof. Sophie Leroy's Attention Residue Lab
bullets: Your brain cannot snap cleanly between unfinished loops
Neural bandwidth stays stuck on the message you just read
scenes.narration: Business professor Sophie Leroy proved why in a landmark lab study. She called it Attention Residue. When you switch from deep work to check one message, part of your working memory stays stuck behind.

scenes.headline: Why 4 Quick Checks Ruin an Entire Morning
scenes.left_body: Check inbox every 15m -> permanent cognitive static
scenes.right_body: Zero open loops -> 100% bandwidth on 1 high-value asset
scenes.narration: Even after you look back at your main task, your brain operates with a steep cognitive penalty while clearing that leftover residue. Four quick checks in two hours means zero deep output.

scenes.headline: The Out-of-Sight 90-Minute Protocol
scenes.stat_subtext: Phone in another room -> 3x faster asset output
scenes.narration: Use the Out-of-Sight Protocol: place your phone inside a closed drawer in another room for one ninety-minute block every morning before opening email.

scenes.headline: Guard the Seal on Your First 90 Minutes
bullets: Physical distance beats willpower every single morning
Ship one real asset before opening any inbox
